intro.x: Simulation turns probability theory into an experimental tool. Given a source of independent uniform random variables (Theorem 15.22), we can generate any distribution, estimate expectations, and measure the error of the estimate. This chapter shows the standard methods and why they work.

blocks.x: Inverse transform
Let $F$ be any CDF and define the generalised inverse $F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$ for $u\in(0,1)$. If $U\sim U(0,1)$ then $X=F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$.

By right-continuity of $F$, $F^{-1}(u)\le x\iff u\le F(x)$. (If $u\le F(x)$ then $x$ belongs to the set whose infimum is $F^{-1}(u)$. Conversely if $F^{-1}(u)\le x$ then by right-continuity the infimum is attained, $F(F^{-1}(u))\ge u$, and $F$ is non-decreasing.) Hence $\Prob(X\le x)=\Prob(U\le F(x))=F(x)$.

Exponential: $F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$, $F^{-1}(u)=-\ln(1-u)/\lambda$; since $1-U\sim U$, use $X=-\ln U/\lambda$. Discrete: with $p_1,\dots,p_m$, return the smallest $k$ with $U\le p_1+\dots+p_k$. Geometric: $X=\lceil\ln U/\ln(1-p)\rceil$.
Rejection sampling
Suppose the target has density $f$ that is hard to invert, but there is a proposal density $g$ we can sample and a constant $M$ with $f(x)\le Mg(x)$ for all $x$.
Repeat: draw $Y\sim g$ and $U\sim U(0,1)$ independently; accept $Y$ if $U\le f(Y)/(Mg(Y))$. The accepted value has density $f$, and the number of trials until acceptance is geometric with mean $M$.

One trial accepts with probability $\int g(y)\frac{f(y)}{Mg(y)}dy=\frac1M$. For a set $A$, $\Prob(Y\in A,\text{accept})=\int_Ag(y)\frac{f(y)}{Mg(y)}dy=\frac1M\int_Af$. Dividing, $\Prob(Y\in A\given\text{accept})=\int_Af$. Trials are independent, so the number of trials is geometric$(1/M)$.

The expected cost is $M$ proposals per sample, and $M\ge1$ with equality iff $f=g$. In dimension $d$, natural proposals have $M$ growing exponentially in $d$ (e.g. sampling a ball by rejection from its bounding cube: acceptance probability $\to0$ super-exponentially), the “curse of dimensionality”.
Special methods
Normal: Box–Muller (Chapter 8), $Z_1=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos2\pi U_2$, $Z_2=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin2\pi U_2$.
Multivariate normal: if $\Sigma=LL^\top$ (Cholesky) and $Z$ has i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ entries then $\mu+LZ\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)$ since $\Cov(LZ)=LL^\top$.
Poisson process: cumulate i.i.d. exponential gaps (Chapter 13).

Non-homogeneous Poisson process by thinning: to simulate rate $\lambda(t)\le\bar\lambda$, generate a homogeneous process at rate $\bar\lambda$ and keep each point at time $t$ independently with probability $\lambda(t)/\bar\lambda$. This is correct by the thinning theorem (Chapter 13), extended to time-dependent retention.

Random permutation (Fisher–Yates): for $i=n,\dots,2$ swap position $i$ with a uniform position in $\{1,\dots,i\}$. It yields every permutation with probability $1/n!$ since there are $n\cdot(n-1)\cdots2=n!$ equally likely choice sequences, each giving a distinct result.
Markov chains: apply the transition row with inverse transform at each step.
To estimate $\theta=\Exp[h(X)]$, draw $X_1,\dots,X_n$ i.i.d. and use $\hat\theta_n=\frac1n\sum h(X_i)$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Properties of the Monte Carlo estimator

blocks.x: Assume $\sigma^2=\Var(h(X))<\infty$. Then
$\Exp\hat\theta_n=\theta$ (unbiased) and $\Var\hat\theta_n=\sigma^2/n$;
$\hat\theta_n\to\theta$ almost surely (strong law);
$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2)$ (CLT), so an approximate $95\%$ confidence interval is $\hat\theta_n\pm1.96\,s_n/\sqrt n$, where $s_n$ is the sample standard deviation.
Linearity and independence give (i); (ii) and (iii) are the SLLN and CLT of Chapter 11; $s_n\to\sigma$ a.s. and Slutsky’s theorem justify the studentised interval.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the $1/\sqrt n$ rate is dimension free

blocks.x: The error is of order $\sigma/\sqrt n$ whatever the dimension of $X$—the main advantage over grid quadrature, whose error degrades with dimension. To gain one extra digit of accuracy requires $100$ times more samples, so the practical lever is reducing $\sigma$.

With $(X,Y)$ uniform on $[-1,1]^2$, $h=\indic_{X^2+Y^2\le1}$ has mean $\pi/4$ and variance $\tfrac\pi4(1-\tfrac\pi4)\approx0.169$. The estimator $4\hat\theta_n$ has standard error $4\sqrt{0.169/n}\approx1.64/\sqrt n$; with $n=10^6$ expect about $3$ correct decimal places ($\approx0.0016$).
Antithetic variables

Use $U$ and $1-U$ in pairs: $\hat\theta=\frac12(h(U)+h(1-U))$. Then $\Var\hat\theta=\tfrac14\bigl(2\sigma^2+2\Cov(h(U),h(1-U))\bigr)=\tfrac12\sigma^2(1+\rho)$ where $\rho$ is the correlation. For monotone $h$, $h(U)$ and $h(1-U)$ are negatively correlated (a consequence of the Chebyshev association inequality, cited), so $\rho\le0$ and the variance of a pair is at most $\sigma^2/2$—no worse than two independent draws.
Control variates

Suppose $W$ has known mean $\Exp W=w$ and is correlated with $h(X)$. For any $c$, $h(X)-c(W-w)$ is unbiased with variance $\sigma^2-2c\Cov(h,W)+c^2\Var W$, minimised at $c^*=\Cov(h,W)/\Var W$, with minimum $\sigma^2(1-\rho^2)$ (the same algebra as linear regression, Chapter 10).
Importance sampling
To estimate $\Exp_f[h(X)]=\int hf$, sample from a different density $g$ (positive wherever $hf\ne0$) and weight:
\Exp_f[h(X)]=\int h(x)\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}g(x)\,dx=\Exp_g\Bigl[h(Y)\frac{f(Y)}{g(Y)}\Bigr].

The variance under $g$ is $\Exp_g[h^2f^2/g^2]-\theta^2$. By Cauchy–Schwarz / Jensen, it is minimised by $g^*\propto\abs hf$, where it equals $(\Exp_f\abs h)^2-\theta^2$ (zero for $h\ge0$, though $g^*$ requires knowing $\theta$). In practice importance sampling is essential for rare events.

Estimate $p=\Prob(Z>5)\approx2.87\times10^{-7}$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Naive Monte Carlo needs $\sim10^{9}$ samples to see a few hits. Sample $Y=5+E$ with $E\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$, density $g(y)=e^{-(y-5)}$ on $y>5$. The weight is $f(y)/g(y)=\phi(y)e^{y-5}$, and $p=\Exp_g[\phi(Y)e^{Y-5}]$, with the integrand bounded by $\phi(5)\approx1.5\times10^{-6}$ and varying slowly over the region, giving a relative error of order $1/\sqrt n$ with a modest constant.
Stratified sampling

Partition the space into strata of known probability and sample within each; the variance equals the within-stratum variance only (by the law of total variance, Chapter 10), never more than naive sampling with proportional allocation.

Often we cannot sample from the target $\pi$ directly (e.g. the normalising constant is unknown). MCMC constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is $\pi$ and whose long-run averages converge to $\Exp_\pi[h]$ (ergodic theorem, Chapter 12).
Let $q(x,y)$ be a proposal kernel. From state $x$, propose $y\sim q(x,\cdot)$ and accept with probability
\alpha(x,y)=\min\Bigl(1,\frac{\pi(y)q(y,x)}{\pi(x)q(x,y)}\Bigr),
otherwise stay at $x$. Then the resulting chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$, hence $\pi$ is stationary.
For $x\ne y$ the transition density is $P(x,y)=q(x,y)\alpha(x,y)$. Then
\pi(x)q(x,y)\alpha(x,y)=\min\bigl(\pi(x)q(x,y),\ \pi(y)q(y,x)\bigr),

which is symmetric in $(x,y)$, so $\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)P(y,x)$. Summing (integrating) over $x$ gives $\pi P=\pi$ as in Chapter 12. Only the ratio $\pi(y)/\pi(x)$ is needed, so $\pi$ need be known only up to a constant.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: what MCMC does and does not guarantee

blocks.x: Stationarity is not enough: the chain must be irreducible and aperiodic for convergence, and mixing speed (how long until the chain forgets its start) can be exceedingly slow if the target is multimodal. Samples are correlated, so the effective sample size is $n/(1+2\sum_k\rho_k)$, where $\rho_k$ is the lag-$k$ autocorrelation. Initial “burn-in” samples are discarded in practice.
The Gibbs sampler updates one coordinate at a time from its full conditional; it is a special case of Metropolis–Hastings with acceptance probability $1$.
Give an inverse-transform sampler for the Pareto law $F(x)=1-x^{-a}$, $x\ge1$, and for the Cauchy law.
Show how to sample the standard normal by rejection from the double-exponential density $g(x)=\tfrac12e^{-\abs x}$ and find the optimal $M$ ($M=\sqrt{2e/\pi}\approx1.32$).
Verify the Fisher–Yates claim by induction on $n$.
Prove the thinning algorithm for non-homogeneous Poisson processes by computing the number of points in $[0,t]$.
Estimate $\int_0^1e^{x}dx$ with antithetic variates and compute the variance reduction factor exactly (target $e-1$).
Design an importance sampler for $\Prob(S_{100}>60)$ for the sum of 100 fair-coin $\pm1$ steps using an exponentially tilted Bernoulli.
Show that Gibbs sampling for the bivariate normal with correlation $\rho$ is a Markov chain with autoregressive coefficient $\rho^2$ for each coordinate, and hence the mixing slows as $\abs\rho\to1$.
